desc:
Encoding. A singly linked list is passed to your function as an array holding the node values from head to tail; an empty array is an empty list. You may build real nodes from it first, or work on the array directly. Lists you return are given as arrays of values from head to tail.

The list is sorted in non-decreasing order. Delete nodes so that every value appears exactly once (keep the first node of each run of equal values) and return the values of the resulting list.

For [1,1,2,3,3,3,4] the answer is [1,2,3,4]. Use the fact that equal values are neighbours: no hash set is needed.
constraints: nums is sorted in non-decreasing order
hints: Because the list is sorted, all copies of a value sit next to each other.
Compare each node only with the node right after it.
Walk with one pointer cur. While cur.next has the same value as cur, unlink it with cur.next = cur.next.next and stay on cur; otherwise step forward.
editorial: Since the list is sorted, duplicates form contiguous runs. Stand on the first node of a run and keep unlinking the following node while it has the same value. Once the next value differs, step forward. The head is always kept, so no dummy node is needed.

Every node is looked at once: O(n) time and O(1) extra space. A hash set would also work but wastes memory and ignores the ordering. Be careful not to advance cur after an unlink, otherwise runs of three or more equal values are only partly removed.
